title: JGB yield curve model — spot yields, risk-neutral rates and term premia
date: Model vintage 19 July 2026 · monthly, July 2002 – July 2029
standfirst: The JMA yield-curve model's own output: fitted zero-coupon JGB yields split into the part explained by expected future policy rates and the part that is compensation for holding duration. Six maturities, monthly from 2002, with the JMA baseline projection to 2029.
stamp: Model vintage: 19 July 2026. Estimates are revised periodically, and updated estimates are available for paid users upon request.
intro_html: The JMA yield curve model splits each JGB yield into interest-rate expectations and a term premium, letting Japan’s long-run interest rate move with its fundamentals. If you are new to this page, a fuller explanation of the model sits at the bottom, and the full argument is in our report, The Long Climb in JGB Yields Is Nearly Over. The charts below are interactive. Hover for exact values, zoom, and download the data behind each chart.
_note: ALTERNATIVE LAYOUT of jgb-yield-curve-model for side-by-side comparison (Takuji, 2026-07-30): decomposition-led exhibit run (10Y then 5/20/30/40Y in parallel), curve + forecast table, then the TP-by-maturity and policy-rate charts; the ACM comparison is embedded in the About section after the block that argues it (its closing sentence reads 'below', not 'above', accordingly). Unlisted — reachable by URL, off the landing page. Every CSV is read from the original pages by relative path (single-copy pattern); same 19 July 2026 vintage throughout.

about.heading: About the model
about.lead: In our reading, most of the historic rise in JGB yields between 2022 and 2026 came from a higher expected path of policy rates and a normalization of term premia as the BoJ withdrew its unconventional easing. Term premia at the longer end have largely finished normalizing, and our forecast sees the Long Climb in JGB yields nearly over. The blocks below explain the model behind that reading.

blocks.head: What the model is.
blocks.text: Our model is a variant of Adrian, Crump and Moench (2013), the standard framework for splitting a bond yield into a risk-neutral component and a term premium. We make one Japan-specific modification. A standard model assumes the economy’s long-run interest rate is stable. Following Bauer and Rudebusch (2020), we let the underlying stars move over time, anchoring the long-run rate to the equilibrium real rate plus trend inflation expectations, each measured for Japan from published sources. Term premia are benchmarked against their 2004 to 2012 averages, the last era of free JGB pricing.

blocks.head: Why we do not use a standard model.
blocks.text: A model with a fixed long-run rate has no place to record Japan’s post-2022 rise in inflation expectations except in the term premium. It therefore reads a genuine repricing of expected rates as a surge in risk compensation. We have seen estimates of a surging JGB term premium circulating in the market. In our judgement they mostly come from standard models and significantly overestimate the premium. As of mid-July 2026, a standard model puts the 10-year term premium around 1.2%. Our estimate reads 0.6% to 0.7%. The chart below shows the difference.

blocks.head: What goes in.
blocks.text: Every input is public. The yield curve data come from the Ministry of Finance and the JSDA. Our equilibrium real rate is a weighted average of the natural-rate estimates compiled by the Bank of Japan. Our trend inflation expectations extend the BoJ’s Composite Index of Inflation Expectations. The value is not in the ingredients. It is in the combination, the estimation choices behind it, and the maintenance of a current, consistent series.

blocks.head: What we publish, and what we do not.
blocks.text: This page carries monthly estimates of spot yields, risk-neutral rates and term premia at 2, 5, 10, 20, 30 and 40 years, from 2002, together with a three-year forecast of the spot curve. The estimation architecture, the parameter choices, and the adjustments that make the model behave are proprietary. We describe what the model does and why. We do not publish how. Readers who want to test our estimates against their own models are welcome to download the data on this page.

references_html: Adrian, Crump & Moench (2013), “Pricing the Term Structure with Linear Regressions,” Journal of Financial Economics, 2013, vol. 110, issue 1, 110-138. This is the base model. The New York Fed publishes daily ACM term-premium estimates for US Treasuries at its “Treasury Term Premia” data page.

Bauer & Rudebusch (2020), “Interest Rates Under Falling Stars,” American Economic Review vol. 110, issue 5, 1316-54. It is seminal paper demostrating the legitimacy of time-varying r* and π* as determinants of the yield curve.

Bank of Japan Monetary Affairs Department, “Developments in the Natural Rate of Interest and the Assessment of the Degree of Monetary Accommodation”. BoJ Review 2026-E-4 — the six natural-rate estimates our r* draws on.

Osada & Nakazawa (BoJ, 2024), “Assessing Measures of Inflation Expectations: A Term Structure and Forecasting Power Perspective”, BoJ Review 2024-E-4. The Composite Index of Inflation Expectations (BoJ-CIE), the basis of our π*, was published in 2024. It has not been officially updated, although we have seen BoJ officials use an updated image chart.

charts.title: 10-year JGB yield: risk-neutral component and term premium
charts.subtitle: 10Y spot yield decomposed into expected policy rates and the term premium
charts.source: Source: JMA JGB yield-curve model, vintage 19 July 2026. Lightened bars and the dotted line from August 2026 = JMA baseline projection.
charts.note: The two blocks sum to the black line at every point. Interest rate expectations are the average short-term rate the market expects over the bond's life; the term premium is the extra it demands for bearing duration and other risks. A negative term premium hangs below the zero line, so the yield sits below the top of the blue block.
